title: The Paradox of Political Outrage
gist: An FP Live event page previewing political historian Anton Jäger's concept of 'hyperpolitics' — the observation that today's digital outrage and cultural signaling on both left and right feel prevalent but fleeting, lacking the backing of the stable parties, unions, and churches that once translated popular energy into durable political power.

insights.claim: Anton Jäger's 'hyperpolitics' framework holds that digital outrage and cultural signaling on both the left and right today are prevalent and simultaneously fleeting, without the backing of stable parties — helping explain how public movements surge and then vanish without changing any underlying sources of power.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: A named analytical framework ('hyperpolitics') for interpreting why viral political movements and online outrage cycles increasingly fail to translate into durable institutional or policy change — useful lens for assessing the staying power of any given protest or social-media-driven political moment before assuming it will move markets or policy.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Popularized by political historian Anton Jäger'

insights.claim: What's missing from today's political movements, per the hyperpolitics thesis, are the parties, unions, and churches that once harnessed popular energy into sustained political power.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific missing institutional intermediaries (parties, unions, churches) as the causal mechanism behind weakened follow-through of modern protest movements — relevant for assessing which populist or protest-driven political risks are likely to fizzle versus those anchored by durable organizations.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Popularized by political historian Anton Jäger'
